prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because it is the sort of surprise I value, but the opening ballots show that the optical lattice clock is the candidate where scientific merit, attribution and maturity all line up best. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem, and Ye's group and several other laboratories have realised clocks near 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, with mutually consistent international comparisons. The result is quantitative and reproducible, which I weigh heavily. It also has consequences beyond metrology: tests of time dilation over millimetres, constraints on drifting constants, and a path to redefining the second. The two-name credit is clean, with the original concept and the decisive realisation. Six of seven members who ranked it placed it in their top three, which gives it a broader base than any rival.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology has been recognised repeatedly (frequency combs 2005, ion clocks 2012), and Ye already shared the 2005 prize, so some will see this as an incremental step on a recognised line rather than a new discovery of nature. It is also a technique rather than a new state of matter or new quantum behaviour, which is where my own taste lies. Credit from other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, Ludlow and Oates, Takamoto) is real, and I am outside my own field here, so I rely on colleagues in atomic physics for priority questions.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as a fundamental advance, a natural continuation of the comb and ion-clock prizes, with Katori and Ye as a clean pair and others in a secondary role; she ranks magic-angle graphene seventh as premature because the superconducting mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I accept most of this. Her argument that the clean two-person credit and the multi-laboratory 1e-18 comparisons make the clock mature is stronger than I gave it credit for, and I have moved it from my seventh place to first. I still disagree with the premature label for twisted bilayer graphene: the existence of flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity has been reproduced widely, and an unsettled pairing mechanism did not stop earlier prizes for cuprate or quantum Hall discoveries. I would, though, ask her to say whether she thinks the Ludlow and Oates stability results change the Ye attribution.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention that overcame Scherzer's limit, but ranks twisted bilayer graphene last on youth and an unresolved mechanism, and notes that Cao as first author cannot be credited.
responses.response: I share her view of the corrector trio, which I ranked fourth: it is mature and reproducible, and its EELS and atomic-resolution data are what my own theory is tested against. I am less sure it is the strongest first choice, because the committee must decide whether it is physics or instrumentation and Krivanek's STEM corrector work complicates priority. I agree that the missing Cao credit is a real weakness for B046, and it is one reason I no longer put it first.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class first as a simple, universal and exactly solvable mechanism with clean liquid-crystal experiments, and places magic-angle graphene fourth because the pairing explanation is not yet stable.
responses.response: I find the KPZ case scientifically beautiful, with exact solutions and quantitative experiments. My reservation is breadth: only he supports it, the exact-solution contributors (Spohn, Sasamoto, Corwin and others) are outside the credited names, and the 1986 theory has been confirmed mostly in specialised settings. I would like to hear which independent experiments beyond Takeuchi and Sano he considers decisive before treating it as a serious rival.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clock first as a textbook case of a technique that moves the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, with quantifiable uncertainties and a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree, and his emphasis on quantifiable, independently checked uncertainties is the same criterion I apply to electronic-structure reproducibility. Where I would qualify his view is that the precedents he lists mean the citation should stress what the lattice scheme enables, namely many-atom stability and relativistic tests, so that the prize does not read as a repeat of 2005 and 2012.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as a distinct achievement given the 2005 and 2012 precedents, and how strongly the Ye overlap with 2005 should count.
Whether other lattice-clock groups' contributions undermine the clean Katori and Ye split.
Whether magic-angle graphene should wait for resolution of the pairing mechanism, and how the missing experimental first author is handled.
Whether a two-part prize pairing a metrology achievement with a condensed-matter one is feasible without exceeding three people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My Uppsala theory work is computationally connected to electron spectroscopy and 2D materials, but this involves no personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals.
